actionThatDiffers: Answer all five blocked prompts in one sitting from a single list instead of discovering them one at a time while tab-cycling; nothing about WHICH answer you give changes.
why: A queue of blocked sessions is a set-membership composite over inputs each individually visible in its own pane; a capture-pane loop yields an adequate approximation of who is waiting, so access caps at 60 (rules 2 and 3). Impact is scheduling convenience, not a changed decision: the same five prompts get the same five answers, just batched. Value also leans on B3 (what it wants) to be worth opening as a queue. High commodity risk: multi-session panes and agent lists are exactly where harness vendors are already heading, and needs-input detection is Claude-only heuristic today.

actionThatDiffers: Stop re-starting locally a task a cloud agent is already running, because you saw the cloud row next to the local rows.
why: Both halves are already reachable: cloud runs sit in a web UI the user knows to click, local runs sit in panes. The item is the merge, not new data, so it is a two-source union a user can approximate by keeping a browser tab open; access lands mid-scale. Impact is mild duplicate-work avoidance. Worst commodity exposure on this board: cloud session state is the vendor OWN data and unifying local plus cloud in one client is squarely on their roadmap, so a native version inside a year is likely rather than speculative.

actionThatDiffers: Stop or throttle the ONE session consuming the window instead of pausing all of them or pausing none and hitting the wall mid-run.
why: No harness attributes shared quota to a session; quota is shown as one account figure. The raw per-message token counts exist in transcripts, but attributing a rolling window across concurrent sessions is a correlate-across-sessions-and-time job most people will not do reliably, so access sits in the 61-80 band. Impact is the strongest of these nine: it names a concrete different action with real loss at stake (a blown window mid-run), and heavy users hit that regularly. Detector flag true because the number rests on a consumption model (cache discounts, model weights, window boundaries) rather than on a revealed figure, so a wrong attribution kills the wrong session.

actionThatDiffers: None I can name. You read a dollar figure after the fact; on a subscription the marginal cost is already sunk and quota, not dollars, is the binding constraint.
why: This is already commodity. Claude Code has a cost command, and one widely known npx tool reads the same transcripts and prints per-session cost, so it is one command away in a place users know to look. Impact is the clearest rule-1 failure on the board: the stated outcome is know what a run costs, which is a feeling, not a decision. Subscription users cannot act on dollars at all, and API users who can already have the tooling.

actionThatDiffers: Answer the longest-starved session first rather than in whatever order you happen to cycle tabs.
why: Shipped, judged as if it did not exist. Duration is a time correlation, but adequate approximations are one loop away: tmux list-panes exposes per-pane activity, and stat on a transcript file gives a good-enough blocked-since, so rule 2 caps this at 60. Impact is thin: when five sessions are blocked the user clears them in the same few minutes regardless of order, and age is a WORSE priority signal than importance, which the board does not know. It sharpens ordering, it does not prevent loss.

actionThatDiffers: Defer starting a large run until after the window resets instead of starting it and losing it half-finished. Real, but the informal version already fires: the usage command says 20 percent left and the user already declines the big refactor.
why: Nothing computes this, which lifts access, but the adequate approximation is cheap and already habitual: remaining quota is one command away and the rest is judgement, so I do not put it in the 81-100 band. Impact is capped by the prediction being about an UNSTARTED task, whose size is the least knowable input in the system. A probability that is wrong even a quarter of the time gets ignored after the second false alarm, and once ignored the delta over eyeballing the usage line is near zero. Strong detector dependence: this is a forecast, not a reveal.

actionThatDiffers: Convert four ad-hoc sessions into a staged workflow with gates, so you stop re-deciding the order by hand each time you return.
why: Kind is action: the deliverable is a thing the user DOES (accept a suggestion, run the commission flow, type one prompt). That is one prompt away today, which rule 5 puts at 21-40, so access is low regardless of how clever the detection is. Impact is where I am harsh: converting to a workflow is a heavyweight commitment tied to one specific orchestration product, and most users will decline the offer and keep hand-driving. It changes practice materially for the minority who accept. Detector flag true because these four are one project is inferred from directory and prompt overlap and will mis-cluster.

actionThatDiffers: None that is new. macOS Focus and Do Not Disturb already suppress notifications for a chosen block, one click away, and the user who wants deep work already reaches for it.
why: Kind is action: flipping a window setting. Rule 5 puts an existing-toggle action at 21-40, and here a full substitute is already shipped by the operating system, so I go to the bottom of that band. Impact is near zero delta: this is a setting ON TOP OF a notification feature, so its whole value is undoing a problem the same product introduced. Nothing about which session you attend to, or when, changes because the mute lives in one app instead of the OS.

actionThatDiffers: None directly. The stated outcome is that four OTHER items become possible, which is an admission that no user action follows from this item itself.
why: Access is genuinely at the top: no harness retains queryable cross-session history, and unlike every other item here the gap is not correlation difficulty but non-recording. You cannot reconstruct by hand what was never written down, at any effort level. But rule 1 binds hard on impact: an enabler whose payoff is other features is a platform bet, and the user does nothing differently the day it lands. It should be BUILT for the four items it unlocks and scored for what it alone changes, which is nothing. Detector flag true: the history is a log of heuristic observations (state badges, activity guesses), so its later value inherits every detector error it recorded.
